articles.title: Theatre company leads way to keep mums on stage
articles.summary: A theatre company is providing childcare to help performers stay on stage after having children.
articles.body:
"It's so special to be given the opportunity to not choose between motherhood and career. It should be the norm," says Finetta Sidgwick.

She is a dancer and is 14 weeks pregnant. Thanks to a special theatre company in Essex, she is still taking to the stage.

The Rhiannon Faith Company (RFC) is paying for childcare and supporting performers with young families, including helping one dancer take her children on tour.

The Harlow-based company says practical support can help talented performers continue their careers without having to choose between work and family life.

But Parents in Performing Arts says more needs to be done across the industry, particularly for freelancers who struggle to find affordable childcare outside traditional hours.

Although RFC was set up in 2019, artistic director Rhiannon Faith has been paying to support performers since 2017 - when she was an independent choreographer.

Since then, she has helped seven mums and one dad.

Sidgwick has received support while rehearsing for Mary Mary, which premieres at Harlow Playhouse next April.

She says the company has provided practical and emotional support, including a pregnancy ball, time to rest and an understudy for performances and the tour.

"I felt that the position of performer was always going to be there, no matter how long my maternity leave was going to be," says the 32-year-old from Brighton, who has been in four other shows since joining RFC in 2021.

About one in five working women have missed out on having a professional job because they became mothers, according to research from the University of Essex.

Performer Shelley Ava Haden, 33, who joined RFC in 2018 and has been in three shows, says childcare is just as important to being able to work.

She has two young children, who were with her during rehearsals, and the company pays for her mother, Carole, to travel with them when she is on tour.

Haden, from the Midlands, is still breastfeeding, while her partner works full-time, meaning there would otherwise be little option for childcare.

"First of all, you just don't feel like a burden," she says.

"I couldn't have done it without the support, I would have had to say no to dance."

The company also provides accommodation with facilities suitable for a family and a childcare payment to recognise the work her mother is doing.

Alongside Sidgwick, Haden was supported by the theatre group while pregnant in 2023.

Faith says supporting performers with families is about retaining some of the most skilled people in the industry.

But she says smaller companies can struggle to afford the support without using their own reserves.

"People are putting off starting families to maintain their career in the arts, and really that's unspeakable," she says.

"If we don't make a ground-breaking shift in financial support for women who want to start families and work in the arts, then the biggest talent in the UK in our industry is going to disappear from our stages."

Without such a shift, she warns: "They're going to be erased from our stories, they're going to be erased off stages."

Parents in Performing Arts says companies are increasingly introducing measures such as flexible hours, job shares and schedules designed around school drop-offs and pick-ups.

But it says childcare remains one of the biggest barriers, particularly because around three quarters of people working in the performing arts are freelancers.

"You don't see the performer sitting there with a calculator going, 'Can I afford to work?'" says Cassie Raine, from Parents in Performing Arts.

"What people are having to do is make that choice all the time: do I continue my career, or do I care for my family?"

Rhiannon Faith says wider financial support is needed so smaller companies can offer similar help.

The BBC has contacted the Department for Culture, Media and Sport for comment.

articles.title: Forever chemicals at former Oxfordshire fuel depot 'have been removed'
articles.summary: Barrels of forever chemicals left at a development site have been removed, a developer has said.
articles.body:
Barrels of chemicals left at an approved development site have been removed and testing carried out, a developer has said.

The Islip Fuel Depot in Oxfordshire is a former RAF and Esso fuel storage and transfer facility and has had outline planning permission approved to build residential and affordable homes.

Concerns were raised after campaigners discovered about 40 barrels of firefighting foam liquid, which contains PFAS - a group of chemicals often dubbed forever chemicals, had been left at the site for decades.

Developer, Newcore, said it had already identified the potential contamination and that "this potential risk and any contamination identified will be cleaned up immediately."

The depot previously supplied fuel to the former RAF Upper Heyford, around five miles north, which is suspected to be the source of forever chemical, or PFAS, contamination from firefighting foam.

Images show the barrels to be manufactured by Angus Fire Armour, that settled a legal battle out of court with residents in Yorkshire, after claims they had been exposed to PFAS near the company's foam manufacturing plant.

CEO of Newcore, Hugo Llewelyn, who took over the site in 2012, said it plans to regenerate the site with 50% affordable housing and that it was made aware of the barrels "in recent weeks" and had them removed in a "responsible and professional manner".

"Whilst firefighting foam containers were present on site from the MOD's operation back in the 20th Century, we do not believe it was ever deployed; the containers were sealed; and successive surveys have confirmed that there is no "pathway" for it to cause pollution," he added.

Mr Llewelyn disputes the quality of the testing carried out by campaigners.

"A 'pressure group' has trespassed unlawfully to obtain a questionable sample from this site to demonstrate that in the secured area of the site that was purposefully designed to accommodate foam for firefighting purposes, which is likely to contain PFAS, does, according to their findings, contain PFAS.

"I'm not sure there is anything to be surprised about here," he said.

He added that a Phase 1 assessment of the site last year had already identified the potential for contamination and that, "the specification for the Phase 2 investigation has therefore been designed to specifically address this potential risk and any contamination identified will be cleaned up immediately".

The Environment Agency's Chemical Compliance team had contacted the site owners to ensure that the drums are properly managed.

Campaigners from Gallos Brook community group, who have been regularly testing for PFAS in the area, took a sample of soil near the storage area which they claimed is "likely the highest level of soil contamination measured anywhere in the UK."

The group said the sample, which was analysed by a UKAS certified laboratory, came back as having 3,743.3 micrograms of PFAS per kilo. PFOS - a particular forever chemical - was found in their testing to be 205 times higher than the safe limit for residential land use.

Llewelyn disputed the testing carried out by campaigners and produced his own results which he claimed were taken from the same area, as part of the Phase 2 investigations.

He said these produced a total level of 64.1 micrograms per kilo of PFAS, roughly 98% lower than results by the campaigners, and were "the accurate results of our professional testing."

The BBC has not been presented with the official lab results to verify these independently.

articles.title: 'Terminal prostate cancer has taught me one lesson I want to pass on'
articles.summary: A Gloucestershire man with terminal cancer shares the life lessons he wishes he'd learned sooner.
articles.body:
A man living with terminal cancer says his biggest regret is spending decades carrying childhood trauma without realising it was shaping his life.

Rex Mackrill, 65, from Tetbury, Gloucestershire, says being diagnosed with incurable prostate cancer forced him to reflect on what matters most, and one lesson he wished he learned earlier: to relish the joy of every moment.

"I knew there was something wrong. I knew there was a blackness that I was carrying and I didn't know what it was, and I wish I'd known earlier," he said.

With a limited time left ahead of him, Rex has been looking back on his life and considering what advice he would pass on.

Football club makes history with £1m lottery win

Headlines: A royal visit and 'shin-kicking'

Traitors star coming to Cheltenham Literature Fest

Because prostate cancer runs in his family, Rex regularly monitored his PSA levels.

After a raised test result, further investigations confirmed he had incurable stage four prostate cancer.

Rex underwent chemotherapy but said the treatment took a significant physical toll and he now lives with the side effects of hormone treatment, including intense fatigue.

"I stopped doing a job I love as a GP practice manager," he said.

"By the time I went through chemotherapy, I couldn't do the job that was needed."

Leaving work was one of the biggest practical changes brought about by his diagnosis, although he says his priorities remain firmly focused on his family.

"Sarah and I have always had a strong focus on our boys. We structured our lives to give them the best upbringing we could."

But while cancer changed his perspective and future plans, he says one of the most important discoveries of his life came years before.

For much of his adult life, Rex lived with anxiety but could not explain why.

"I knew that I was frightened, but I didn't know why," he said.

The turning point came at 60 when a life coach noticed he appeared to "shut down" while discussing certain topics.

"He said, 'You've got trauma, dude'," Rex recalled.

He later sought help and was diagnosed with PTSD.

Rex believes the trauma stemmed from abuse suffered in his childhood and says he is still exploring its impact today.

"I wish I'd known I had a trauma earlier," he said.

Research suggests delayed PTSD diagnoses are not uncommon, with symptoms sometimes emerging years after traumatic events.

Around one in 10 people in the UK are expected to experience PTSD at some point in their lives.

At first, Rex said he struggled to accept help.

But Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) and Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR) therapy gradually transformed the way he experienced life.

"I used to live at 10 out of 10 anxiety and I don't now," he said.

"People would say I was calm and collected, but they weren't aware of the stress and anxiety I carried."

Looking back, he says his advice to anyone struggling is straightforward.

"You don't have to live like that or carry it on your own.

"Go to a trusted friend and say there's something blocking you. They can help you find the support you need."

As he comes to terms with terminal cancer, Rex says his priorities have not changed but what has changed is how present he feels.

"I used to have to go to the Lake District to be present," he said.

"Now I can be much more present wherever I am."

Recently, he found himself captivated by a simple moment outside.

"I was watching rooks floating on the wind," he said.

"One rook wanted to move a little bit along a tree branch, but the wind took it somewhere else.

"It had to circle around and land exactly where it wanted to be."

He now spends time writing poetry, donating possessions like his car to charity and trying to make life easier for those he will leave behind.

"I don't want to burden people with my stuff," he said.

Rex has also taken part in sessions at Longfield Hospice in Minchinhampton that help people discuss end-of-life plans and their wishes for care.

Sarah Mimmack, director of care at the hospice, said many families avoid conversations about death because they find them uncomfortable, but planning ahead can remove uncertainty and pressure.

"If you've done this work before you die, it really helps your family and friends," she said.

She added that while around half of people in the UK die in hospital, only a small proportion say that is where they would choose to spend their final days.

For Rex, however, preparing for death has become another way of making the most of the present.

And if there is one lesson he hopes others take from his experience, it is not to wait.

"Enjoy the joy of life and see that this is a beautiful world we live in," he said.

"We're so lucky. We can love every moment of it."

articles.title: Manx youth music and dance workshop Bree celebrates 20 years
articles.summary: Youth group Bree, is marking 20 years with a two-day music and dance workshop at half term.
articles.body:
For 20 years, youth club Bree has been bringing young people together on the Isle of Man "so they meet each other and start making new friendships and new bands", says founder Dr Chloë Woolley.

The Manx music and dance group, whose name means "vitality", was set up to give children who had never come across traditional music "a fun introduction" to it.

Since then, its young musicians have gone on to play festivals, record albums, perform at the Royal Albert Hall and build professional careers.

Now it is marking its 20th birthday with a two-day workshop this October half term.

Woolley, Culture Vannin's Manx Music Development Officer, has run Bree since it began.

She said it was modelled on Scotland's Fèis movement, which promotes Scottish traditional music.

While some schools taught traditional music, she said, much of the Manx cultural arts was "just invisible" to many young people around the island, so the idea was to bring them together and introduce them to Manx songs, tunes and language.

She said the club brought Manx music to life and aimed "to ensure that Manx music and dance remain a living tradition".

Some former members have gone on to professional music careers, including fiddle player Isla Callister and harpist Mera Royle.

Others have joined Scran, an advanced teenage folk group which has recorded two albums and performed at the Royal Albert Hall.

Woolley said former students often come back to help.

"A lot of students feel like they want to then give back once they're doing quite well professionally," she said.

She said interest in Manx culture had grown over the past two decades, helped this year by Blein ny Gaelgey, the Year of the Manx Language.

The workshop, in St John's, will see young musicians and dancers aged 10 to 18 work on collectively performing a Manx fairy tale.

It costs £20 and is open to singers, dancers and musicians, as well as those who just want to help make props.

It runs from 10:00 to 16:00 on 27 and 28 October, and finishes with a free concert for family and friends.

"You might actually feel this is the first time that you feel brave enough to perform, and feel fantastic and encouraged," Woolley said.

articles.title: Aurigny aircraft standby plan aims to improve reliability
articles.summary: Aurigny bosses say the move could help it have better control of its costs.
articles.body:
An airline is planning to keep one of its planes on standby next year to help when flights are disrupted.

Aurigny said its summer schedule for 2027 aimed to "keep Guernsey well connected" with flights to destinations including London Gatwick, Jersey, Dublin, Edinburgh and Paris.

Within its schedule, the States-owned airline said it was building in more spare capacity with one of its five aircraft being held in reserve to cover any service issues.

Philip Saunders, chief commercial officer of Aurigny, said the airline wanted to "work smarter" with its aircraft to give passengers a more reliable service.

Aurigny said 86% of its flights in 2026 arrived within 15 minutes of schedule.

Saunders added being able to offer a more reliable service could also help the airline have better control of its costs and keep them down.

"Lots of non-productive costs won't arise as a result," he added.

"So everybody wins, the consumer, the airline and most importantly, we'll all be on time to do whatever it is we want to do where we're going."

articles.title: Jersey tops 1m air passengers after summer boost
articles.summary: Ports of Jersey says the figures reflect a strong year for travel to and from the island.
articles.body:
Passenger numbers rose across Jersey's transport hubs during the busy summer months, with more than one million people passing through the airport so far this year, according to official statistics.

Ports of Jersey said more than 472,000 passengers travelled through Jersey Airport between July and September, up 4.2% on the same period in 2025.

Nearly 200,000 passengers travelled through Jersey Harbour, while ferry operator DFDS carried 10% more passengers than it did during the third quarter of last year.

Paul Holley, head of connectivity at Ports of Jersey, said it was "encouraging to see sustained growth".

The figures continue a strong year for travel to and from the island, with Jersey Airport reaching the milestone of its one millionth passenger of 2026 at the end of August.

Holley said: "The third quarter is our busiest period of the year, and it's encouraging to see sustained growth through both our air and sea gateways with visitors making the most of the great Jersey summer.

"This was supported by higher frequencies on key services such as KLM's Amsterdam route, alongside Loganair's first full summer with routes to Bordeaux, East Midlands, Norwich and Paris added to its core network."

During the peak summer season, the airport offered direct flights to 41 destinations across the UK and Europe.

Airlines continued to invest in Jersey's route network, supporting a timetable of up to 185 departing flights a week.

The harbour also reported a positive summer, with DFDS seeing passenger numbers increase across its Jersey routes compared with the same period in 2025.

articles.title: ‘Nuclear weapons not routine instruments of statecraft’: India’s warning to Pakistan at UN
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India on Friday warned Pakistan against using nuclear weapons as a tool of political pressure, asserting that New Delhi would not bow to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Friday warned Pakistan against using nuclear weapons as a tool of political pressure, asserting that New Delhi would not bow to nuclear blackmail and that any terrorist attack against the country would invite a fitting response.Exercising its Right of Reply at the United Nations General Assembly's First Committee, which deals with disarmament and international security, India said nuclear weapons must not be treated as “routine instruments of statecraft”.Senior Adviser (Disarmament) at India's Permanent Mission to the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva, Anmol Sher Singh Bedi, delivered the response following remarks by Pakistan on Jammu and Kashmir.“Jammu and Kashmir is an integral and inalienable part of India,” Bedi said, rejecting Pakistan's claims over the region.He said India's military capabilities were defensive in nature and shaped by its security environment, rather than directed against any particular country.“We heard concerns about escalation. These are legitimate concerns. However, these are best judged by conduct over time. Nuclear weapons must not be treated as routine instruments of statecraft,” Bedi said.He warned that relying on the threat of nuclear weapons to shield activities below the threshold of conventional warfare could increase the risk of escalation rather than promote restraint.“A posture that relies on nuclear overhang to limit the consequences of subconventional activity raises the risk of escalation and not the prospect of restraint,” he said.Bedi also outlined what he described as a recurring pattern in regional crises, involving provocation, denial of responsibility and subsequent appeals for restraint after a response.“Where those in power are neither elected by people nor accountable to them, their decisions carry no risk and impose no cost for those who take them. That is how crisis becomes an instrument of power. That is how instability becomes useful, and that is how the cycle keeps on repeating,” he said.India reiterates three red linesIndia said its position on terrorism and national security remained clear, identifying three principles that would guide its response to threats.“First, any terrorist attack against India will receive a fitting response. Second, India will not bow to nuclear blackmail. Third, India will make no distinction between those who sponsor terrorism and those who mastermind it,” Bedi said.He said India's actions in May 2025 followed a “grave provocation” and were undertaken in self-defence after the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir, in which 26 civilians, mostly tourists, were killed.“These actions were measured, targeted, and designed to be non-escalatory,” Bedi said.India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, 2025, targeting what it described as terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir in retaliation for the Pahalgam attack. The Resistance Front, a proxy of Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba, was linked to the attack.Bedi also stressed that the use of non-state actors by a country did not absolve it of responsibility for their actions.“The use of force by states under the garb of non-state actors does not erase the state's responsibility. India's right of self-defense remains intact,” he said.India raises Indus Waters Treaty, nuclear proliferationIndia also referred to the Indus Waters Treaty, arguing that the agreement depended on mutual trust and cooperation between the two countries.“A state cannot undermine those foundations of trust and cooperation and at the same time insist that the privileges flowing from the relationship remain untouched,” Bedi said.Following the Pahalgam attack, India announced that the treaty would be held in abeyance until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably ended its support for cross-border and other forms of terrorism.On nuclear proliferation, Bedi invoked the legacy of Pakistani nuclear scientist Abdul Qadeer Khan and the international proliferation network associated with him, which supplied nuclear equipment and expertise to countries seeking to develop nuclear weapons.The network contributed to international concerns that led to United Nations Security Council Resolution 1540, adopted in 2004, which requires states to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and their means of delivery to non-state actors.“This is relevant in the context of demands for unquestioned nuclear cooperation and transfer of advanced weapons and military capabilities. We urge all states and all responsible suppliers to exercise the highest degree of vigilance, not because of India, but for their own security,” Bedi said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Massachusetts dairy farmer nearly sold an unfarmable slice of his land to Walmart, but put an 11-acre solar field there instead; the lease paid $1,000 a week while rooftop panels erased a $1,400 monthly power bill
articles.summary: A Massachusetts dairy farmer once considered selling an awkward, hard-to-farm patch of his property to Walmart.
articles.body: A Massachusetts dairy farmer once considered selling an awkward, hard-to-farm patch of his property to Walmart. Instead, he turned the 11-acre slice into a solar field that now provides a steady lease income, while rooftop panels have nearly wiped out the farm’s $1,400 monthly electricity bill. The story was told by John Nagy in Notre Dame Magazine in 'The Sun Farmers', a feature also republished by the Let’s Share the Sun Foundation. It follows George Hunt Jr., whose decision to combine farming with solar power created a new source of income without giving up the land. His experience shows how a property that seemed unsuitable for crops could still contribute to the farm, the local energy supply and the family’s long-term plans. Read on to know more about it here:A difficult piece of farmlandHunt’s farm was a working dairy operation, with hundreds of acres and a herd of about 250 cows. Like many dairy farmers, he had to balance the costs of running the farm against the uncertain returns from milk. He also wanted to leave his children a business that could support a decent quality of life without requiring them to milk an enormous herd every day.One part of the property presented a different kind of challenge. The 11-acre plot was levelled land that was difficult to farm. According to Nagy’s account, Hunt considered selling it to Walmart, which was interested in the site. The retailer’s offer could have turned the unproductive parcel into a straightforward financial gain.But Hunt began to see another possibility. Solar panels could make use of land that was not well suited to growing crops, while allowing the farm to retain ownership. Rather than sell the site outright, he could lease it to a solar developer and earn regular income from the land.The decision did not happen in isolation. Massachusetts had created incentives for solar power, including renewable energy credits, and the state’s solar programme had targets that encouraged development. Those policies helped make solar a viable option for farmers and other landowners.The value of solar on the barnBefore committing to a larger project, Hunt had already installed solar panels on the roof of his barn. The array supplied power for many of the farm’s daily needs, including pumping water, cooling milk, operating milking equipment and running lights.When writer Nagy visited in 2015, he shared in his article that Hunt said the rooftop system had almost eliminated the farm’s monthly electricity bill of about $1,400. It also generated a small refund during much of the year for electricity sent back to the grid. For a dairy farm with substantial energy needs, reducing a major monthly expense offered a practical benefit beyond the environmental appeal of renewable power.The rooftop system gave Hunt confidence to consider a much larger solar project. If panels could help manage the farm’s own electricity costs, a ground-mounted array could make productive use of the land that had little value for conventional farming.Hunt’s experience also highlights the importance of careful advice when navigating a complicated industry. The feature describes solar consultant Bill Jordan reviewing an earlier contract and helping Hunt identify a federal grant that had been overlooked. Hunt offered to pay Jordan for the work, but Jordan returned the check after the original contractor said it would prepare the grant application.Leasing land to harvest sunshineHunt eventually chose solar over selling the awkward parcel to Walmart. The 11-acre site became part of a 3-megawatt solar array that supplied electricity to the city of Lowell, Massachusetts, according to Nagy’s report.The arrangement gave Hunt a land-lease payment of $1,000 a week. While the income was reportedly less than the amount Walmart had offered to buy the land, it provided a recurring return while Hunt kept ownership of the property. The farmer described himself as pleased with the decision and came to see himself as a “sun farmer,” as per the report.That phrase captures the unusual way the project fit into the farm. Hunt continued to raise cows, produce milk and manage the agricultural business, but the leased land created another kind of harvest. Instead of crops, the field produced electricity, while the lease payment supported the farm’s finances.Solar also created opportunities beyond the main array. Hunt was considering additional panels for other buildings on the property, including a structure used as an indoor sports arena. The electricity could serve tenants at a nearby restaurant and help reduce their energy costs.A different kind of farm incomeThe solar lease was particularly valuable because dairy income could fluctuate. As per the report, Hunt told Nagy that farmers might receive a good price for milk only every few years, making it important to find other sources of revenue. His farm already diversified through activities such as selling firewood and hay and investing in local real estate.The solar project added another layer to that approach. It did not replace dairy farming, but gave Hunt a reliable income stream from land that was difficult to use for crops. The rooftop panels, meanwhile, reduced the farm’s operating expenses by addressing one of its largest utility costs.That combination matters. A lease payment can help with income, but avoiding a recurring electricity bill can be just as useful to a business that operates equipment every day. The systems addressed two separate financial pressures: one through revenue from the leased field and the other through lower power costs.Hunt also helped connect other farmers with Jordan, passing along the names of 25 or 30 people interested in solar. The feature notes that successful referrals brought him a small commission. His experience had become a practical example for other landowners weighing whether solar could fit their operations.Keeping the land in the familyFor Hunt, the choice was not simply between Walmart and solar panels. It was about how to make a difficult piece of land work for the farm’s future. Selling would have provided an immediate payment, but leasing the land created recurring income and allowed the family to retain ownership.The rooftop installation also helped make the wider farm more financially resilient. By reducing an electricity bill of about $1,400 a month to almost nothing, the system freed up money that would otherwise have gone to power costs. The 11-acre field added a separate weekly lease payment, giving the farm a second benefit from solar.Hunt’s story offers a grounded example of how renewable energy can fit into an existing business. It did not require him to stop farming or convert the whole property. Instead, the panels occupied land that was hard to farm and helped power homes, businesses and municipal operations elsewhere.A patch of land once considered for a big-box store became part of a local energy project. Hunt kept his farm, gained a weekly lease payment and cut a major monthly expense. In a business where margins can be tight and conditions change from year to year, the sun became another crop worth cultivating.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: From Flight Attendant to Fighter Jet Pilot: Thailand’s Queen Suthida completes her first solo Gripen flight after logging over 1,188 flying hours across military and civilian aircraft
articles.summary: Thailand’s Queen Suthida has added a remarkable achievement to her aviation record by flying a Swedish-made Gripen fighter jet solo for the first time.
articles.body: Thailand’s Queen Suthida has added a remarkable achievement to her aviation record by flying a Swedish-made Gripen fighter jet solo for the first time. The flight, completed at a Royal Thai Air Force base in southern Thailand, marks another step in a journey that has taken her from working as a flight attendant to gaining experience in military aircraft and royal aviation.The Queen flew a single-seat JAS 39C Gripen at Wing 7 air base in Surat Thani province on October 8, with King Maha Vajiralongkorn watching the milestone. Before take-off, she attended a briefing on the flight plan and personally checked the aircraft before proceeding to the runway. After she completed the flight, the King congratulated her with a bouquet and a Gripen Order Golden Patch, an insignia associated with flying the fighter aircraft. The achievement stands out because flying a high-performance fighter jet requires specialised preparation and training. The Queen had already flown the two-seat JAS 39D Gripen before undertaking her first solo flight in the single-seat version.From commercial flights to military aviationQueen Suthida’s path to the cockpit began long before her latest flight. Born on June 3, 1978, in Hat Yai district of Thailand’s Songkhla province, she studied communication arts at Assumption University in Bangkok, graduating in 2000. She subsequently worked as a flight attendant for JALways, a Japan Airlines affiliate, before joining Thai Airways International, where she worked until 2008. Her career later took a different direction when she joined the Royal Security Command and became involved in royal security duties.According to her official biography published by the Thai government, she rose through senior positions in the royal security establishment. In 2017, she held the position of Deputy Commander of the Royal Security Command, with the rank of special general. She married King Maha Vajiralongkorn in May 2019 and was formally bestowed the title of Queen during the royal investiture ceremony that month.Her aviation training developed alongside her military career. She began flying the Cessna T-41D in 2010 and went on to train on several other aircraft, including the CT-4E Airtrainer and Pilatus PC-9. Her experience also includes the Mooney M20M, Piper PA-34 Seneca and Boeing 737 passenger aircraft. The range of aircraft reflects her experience across civilian and military aviation, rather than a career limited to a single type of plane.More than 1,188 hours in the airThe Queen has accumulated 1,188.48 flying hours across different aircraft, according to figures reported by Thai media. These include 315.33 hours on the Cessna T-41, 105.59 hours on the Pilatus PC-9 and more than 480 hours across the Boeing 737-400 and Boeing 737-800. Before her solo Gripen flight, she had also logged 10.13 hours on the two-seat JAS 39D.Her preparation for the solo flight reportedly involved several weeks of training. She made stays in Surat Thani between August and September and again from late September to October 8, during which she trained on a Gripen flight simulator and followed Royal Thai Air Force procedures under expert supervision.The Queen has also served as co-pilot alongside the King on royal flights for official duties in Thailand and overseas. During the royal couple’s visit to Bhutan in April 2025, they jointly operated a royal aircraft that landed at Paro International Airport, known for its demanding approach through mountainous terrain.A milestone in a long aviation journeyQueen Suthida’s first solo flight in the Gripen brings together years of training, flying experience and military service. It is not her first experience in a fighter aircraft, but it marks an important step from flying the two-seat version to operating the single-seat jet alone. Her journey from commercial aviation to military flying also offers a glimpse into the breadth of her professional experience beyond public royal duties. With more than 1,188 hours in the air and experience across several aircraft categories, the solo flight represents the latest achievement in an aviation record built over many years.You use AI every day. articles.title: Palantir AI probe leads to Met Police volunteer chief's dismissal
articles.summary: Special chief officer James Deller copied intimate images on to his work phone, AI monitoring finds.
articles.body:
The Metropolitan Police has fired the head of its Special Constabulary after Palantir's AI monitoring uncovered that he had used his work phone to copy intimate images of a woman.

Special chief officer James Deller, who led the force's volunteer officers, was dismissed following a misconduct hearing on Friday.

The Met said investigators used lawful business monitoring and Palantir's Foundry system, which uses artificial intelligence (AI), to find the misconduct by Deller.

Cdr Pete Stevens said: "SCO Deller failed to meet that bar. His actions were an abuse of the trust put in him and it is right that he is no longer able to serve in policing."

Investigators found that in July and August 2025, Deller used his police-issued phone to take photos of two intimate images that had been sent to his personal phone.

The pictures had been sent using WhatsApp's "view once" feature, which makes them disappear after they are opened.

He then sent the copied images back to his personal device before deleting them from his work phone.

The misconduct was discovered during a week-long operation called Project Galatasaray, which used the AI technology in a bid to identify corruption and professional misconduct within the Met.

Deller will be added to the College of Policing's barred list, meaning he will not be able to serve in policing again.

Stevens added: "The vast majority of Met officers and staff serve London with dedication and integrity, and they rightly expect robust action against the small minority who abuse their position and undermine public trust.

"That is particularly true of those who serve in the Special Constabulary. They are volunteers who selflessly give up their time to keep London safe.

"They deserve to be led by people who demonstrate the highest standards in all parts of their lives."

In April, the Metropolitan Police Federation, which represents rank-and-file officers, urged officers to be "extremely cautious" about carrying Met-issued devices while off duty after the force upgraded its Lawful Business Monitoring software.

The federation's general secretary, Matt Cane, said staff had not been told the upgrade included the introduction of Palantir's artificial intelligence technology, appearing to mark its first deployment to monitor Met systems.

In May, Metropolitan Police Deputy Commissioner Matt Jukes told the London Assembly's Police and Crime Committee that officers were not under any "additional surveillance in the workplace" after the force began using AI in a bid to root out bad behaviour.

He said the Met had considered the reputational risks of using the "divisive" technology, but added that it helped identify "unacceptable, dishonest, corrosive behaviours" among officers.

The London Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime (Mopac) blocked the Met from signing a two-year contract with Palantir to provide artificial intelligence technology for criminal investigations.

Mopac said the force had failed to set out its procurement strategy, describing this as a "clear and serious breach" of procedure.

Palantir is now suing Mopac, alleging it unlawfully blocked the deal after taking the company's "values and ethics" into account, which it said was an "irrelevant consideration.

Palantir, founded by controversial tech billionaire Peter Thiel, holds contracts with a number of UK public bodies, including the NHS and the Ministry of Defence.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is currently facing growing pressure from Labour MPs and trade unions to end government contracts with Palantir.

Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, who recently joined the company , warned against "mob rule" in government procurement.

Lord Watson told BBC Radio 4's Political Thinking With Nick Robinson: "One of the things I'd say to my former colleagues is, 'Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want to let mob rule lead procurement practices?'

"Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one."

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has informed Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke about the death of his grandmother while he remains in detention in the national capital ahead of the party’s proposed protest against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.“It is now up to him whether he wants to stay back and continue the protest under detention or fly back for the last rites,” Delhi Police sources, quoted by news agency ANI said on Saturday.Dipke’s paternal grandmother, Savitribai Shankarrao Dipke, 85, died at her home in Santuk Pimpri village in Maharashtra’s Hingoli district at 11.30am on Saturday following a prolonged illness, family sources told PTI.She had been unwell for about a month and was earlier hospitalised in Hingoli. His parents had been informed and were on their way to the village.He said Dipke had met his grandmother on August 15, when he launched the ‘School Thik Karo’ campaign in Hingoli district, and met her once more afterwards. He had not been able to see her in the last 20-25 days, family sources said.CJP leaders detained ahead of protestDipke, along with CJP co-convenor Saurav Das and leader Ashutosh Ranka, was detained by Delhi Police after arriving in the capital from Mumbai on Saturday.The leaders had travelled to Delhi for the party’s proposed ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ protest demanding Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Delhi Police had denied permission for the demonstration, citing public safety, traffic management and law-and-order concerns. articles.title: In 2024, Michael Bloomberg's foundation gave Johns Hopkins $1 billion; the gift made medical school tuition-free for students from families earning under $300,000 and expanded help with living costs
articles.summary: For many students, getting into medical school is only the beginning of a much bigger financial challenge.
articles.body: For many students, getting into medical school is only the beginning of a much bigger financial challenge. Tuition, accommodation and everyday expenses can make years of professional training difficult to afford. In July 2024, Bloomberg Philanthropies announced a $1 billion gift to Johns Hopkins University to help ease that burden. According to Johns Hopkins University President Ron Daniels’ official announcement, the donation expanded financial aid across graduate programmes, with a major change for medical students: those from families earning less than $300,000 a year became eligible for free tuition, while students from families earning up to $175,000 could receive support for both tuition and living expenses.A donation aimed at reducing the cost of higher educationThe gift came from Bloomberg Philanthropies, founded by Michael R. Bloomberg, who graduated from Johns Hopkins in 1964 with a degree in electrical engineering. The donation was directed towards graduate financial aid, with the university seeking to make advanced education more accessible to students who might otherwise struggle with its cost. This was not Bloomberg’s first major contribution to the institution. In 2018, he pledged $1.8 billion to Johns Hopkins to expand undergraduate financial aid. That donation enabled the university to provide need-based financial aid without requiring students to take out loans as part of their financial aid packages.The 2024 gift focused on students pursuing advanced degrees, including those preparing for careers in medicine, nursing, public health, research and other fields. For Johns Hopkins, the aim was to make sure that a student’s financial background did not become a deciding factor in whether they could pursue further education.How the medical school funding worksThe most significant change was introduced at the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine in autumn 2024. Under the new financial aid arrangements, students from families earning less than $300,000 annually became eligible for tuition-free medical education. A second level of assistance was created for students from families earning up to $175,000 a year. Those who qualified could receive support covering tuition, fees and living expenses.The two thresholds serve different purposes. Students who qualify under the $300,000 limit receive help with tuition, while the broader package for those under the $175,000 threshold also addresses the cost of living during medical training. Johns Hopkins said the $300,000 income limit covered families representing approximately 95% of Americans. The lower threshold for assistance with living expenses covered nearly 85% of US families. The university also estimated that nearly two-thirds of students entering its medical school in autumn 2024 would qualify for either free tuition or the more comprehensive financial aid package.The changes were intended to benefit eligible incoming and returning students, rather than being restricted to those joining the school that year. As with other need-based aid, eligibility depends on students meeting the university’s financial requirements.Support for students beyond medical schoolThe $1 billion gift was not reserved exclusively for future doctors. Johns Hopkins planned to use the funding to expand financial assistance across several graduate programmes. Students at the School of Nursing and the Bloomberg School of Public Health were among those expected to benefit. Other areas included engineering, education, business, arts and sciences, international studies and the Peabody Institute. The university also included its planned School of Government and Policy in its wider graduate education plans.The form of assistance varies by programme. It can include need-based scholarships and fully funded PhD fellowships, helping students manage the cost of studying while pursuing research or professional training. Rather than giving every graduate student the same amount, the university intended to direct financial support through its individual academic divisions. This allowed each school to address the needs of students enrolled in its programmes.Why Michael Bloomberg chose to support educationBloomberg’s own experience as a student has shaped his approach to financial aid. He attended Johns Hopkins with assistance from a federal scholarship programme and earned money through a campus job. His contribution reflects the view that access to education should not depend entirely on a family’s ability to pay. For medical students, in particular, the cost of training can influence how much debt they take on before beginning their careers.Reducing tuition and, for eligible students, covering living expenses could give graduates more flexibility when making decisions about their future. It may also help students consider careers in research, public health and other areas where financial rewards are not always the primary motivation. The university’s wider goal is to attract students with strong academic potential from different economic backgrounds and prepare them for work in fields that serve the public.A lasting commitment to graduate financial aidJohns Hopkins described the $1 billion contribution as a long-term investment in graduate education, with funding intended to support financial aid in perpetuity. The impact goes beyond the headline announcement about medical school tuition. The gift also strengthens assistance for students in selected graduate programmes, including those preparing for careers in healthcare, science, education and public service.Not every student automatically receives free tuition or help with living costs; the benefits depend on family income, financial need and programme eligibility. Even so, the scale of the donation gives Johns Hopkins a substantial source of funding to help students manage the cost of advanced education.For students considering medical school or other graduate degrees, the initiative addresses one of the biggest barriers to pursuing further study: the financial commitment that comes with it.You use AI every day. articles.title: Drumcree: Two deals discussed before parade ban, says Bryant
articles.summary: The decision followed a warning from the chief constable that allowing the procession to go ahead could lead to serious injury, disorder and wider unrest across Northern Ireland.
articles.body:
The Northern Ireland Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant has said his decision to ban the Orange Order's Drumcree march was in the best interests of peace.

He announced the decision on Friday after an agreement couldn't be reached between the Portadown District Lodge and the Garvaghy Road residents.

Sir Chris said he received advice from the the PSNI chief constable that allowing the procession to go ahead could lead to serious injury, disorder and wider unrest across Northern Ireland.

Speaking to BBC News NI, Sir Chris defended his decision after it was put to him that unionists believed it had undermined the rule of law.

"It's my job to try and make sure that we have a peaceful set of outcomes in Northern Ireland," he said. "I didn't come to this decision lightly."

He appealed for a lowering of political tensions.

"I really would urge everybody to stand down any rallies or gatherings that there may be. Nobody wants to wind this up any further.

"There's been, I would argue, too much winding up already over the last couple of weeks.

"It's easy to stir up a sectarian grievance, much more difficult to calm it down.

"But we will need to look at the long term establishment of trust ."

Sir Chris told BBC News NI that the original Parades Commission determination would remain in place, despite his decision to stop the parade.

"I've decided not to strike down the original determination that still stands in law.

"The Orange Order won that right," he continued.

"But I have decided nonetheless that the march should not go ahead, partly because of the significant disruption to community relations that it would represent, partly because of the way in which the police have advised me that it would have to proceed and could lead to significant unrest."

The Court of Appeal has reserved judgment on a legal challenge brought by Garvaghy Road residents against the decision to allow the march.

Sir Chris also outlined two possible compromises that had been discussed in an attempt to resolve the dispute.

One proposed compromise, he said, would have allowed the Orangemen to complete one final march along the Garvaghy Road, on the condition it would not apply to march the route again.

The other would have seen the group accept that it had won the right to march, but agree not to exercise that right.

Sir Chris said he believed an agreement had been close, but talks between the lodge and residents ultimately failed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, he defended his decision to stop the parade, saying he could not see how the procession could safely take place.

He also said Stormont's power-sharing institutions had proved more resilient than expected, despite concerns the dispute could lead to the collapse of the Northern Ireland Executive.

The stalemate has reopened what was once one of the most bitter parading dispute in Northern Ireland, with stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

For decades, the situation at Drumcree has settled into a relatively minor stand-off that no longer made headlines, however that changed when the Parades Commission ruled that the march, on Sunday 27 September, could go ahead with restrictions in place .

That parade did not happen and, after a series of talks between residents and Orangemen, the secretary of state has banned the procession.

Sir Chris said he had spent the last fortnight trying to reach a resolution between Garvaghy Road residents and the Portadown District Lodge, holding a series of negotiations at Hillsborough Castle.

"I thought we were very close to an agreement, but unfortunately that was tantalisingly difficult to achieve."

He explained that two possible compromises had been considered.

"One was what people called one done and dusted. In other words, they would do one march and never apply again."

"And another version was that they would accept that they had won the right, but they wouldn't exercise that right."

Sir Chris said neither proposal had secured agreement from both sides.

He said the Chief Constable Jon Boutcher had written to him requesting intervention under the Public Processions (Northern Ireland) Act 1998.

"But it seemed to me that the real threat was, precisely as the chief constable had outlined, I couldn't see how the procession could take place."

Sir Chris also said he believed the original determination by the Parades Commission to allow the march had been "legitimate".

Asked what he had learned from the dispute during his time as Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Chris said: "It's not the easiest gig in the world."

He said he had encountered people willing to compromise, but others who found it more difficult.

"And I've learned that there are a lot of people of good will who want to make compromise. And there are some people who find compromise much more difficult."

Sir Chris said there had been concerns that the dispute could lead to the collapse of Northern Ireland's power-sharing executive.

However, he said the institutions had remained in place despite the tensions.

"The institutions of the Good Friday Agreement are probably more resilient than people think."

Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes, when stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.

The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches.

Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order for the past three decades.

Earlier this year the Parades Commission decided that the march could go ahead on 27 September with restrictions in place after its original decision to stop the march was overturned in court.

That morning, up to 1,000 people - including politicians such as Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill - blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church a mile to the west.

Since then, residents have maintained a constant presence around the road while Orangemen have also repeatedly tried to march the route before being turned back by police.

On Friday night, members of the Portadown District Lodge again walked to police lines at Drumcree, as they have done regularly over the past two weeks, but were halted.

The chief constable said last week that the consequences of police forcing an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road "could be catastrophic".

He had said while the PSNI's objective was to facilitate the determination, this could not be done "at all costs".

In his application to have Sir Chris review the ruling, Boutcher said that costs were a factor.

"I highlighted that the continuing costs and impact upon the PSNI were significant and in the context of our existing funding challenges could not be sustained indefinitely," he stated.

The PSNI has said the cost of policing the two-week stand-off has been about £5m, but warned that figure could rise.

During the policing operation, about 140 officers were drafted in from across the UK to help under mutual aid arrangements. They have now left Northern Ireland.

The dispute has also prompted a police investigation.

The First Minister Michelle O'Neill confirmed she had received a letter from police investigating protests over Drumcree.

On Thursday, police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview.

Two weeks ago, the Parades Commission issued a determination saying that the Orange Order parade was to be allowed on the Garvaghy Road with restrictions in place.

That prompted a legal challenge from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition which opposed the march.

The Court of Appeal is considering whether to allow a challenge to the Parades Commission's ruling, which has been lodged by residents.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress general secretary KC Venugopal announced that the party-led opposition INDIA bloc would stage a major protest in Delhi on Monday as part of its ongoing campaign to "safeguard people's voting rights.""The Congress and the INDIA bloc will continue their agitation until the electoral process and system were made free and fair," he told reporters in his Lok Sabha constituency, Alappuzha, on Saturday.Alleging that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah were attempting to "shield" Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, Venugopal claimed their efforts would ultimately lead to their "downfall."“PM Modi is behaving like a leader nearing his downfall. He is afraid of the Opposition's protests,” he added.Venugopal further alleged that security curbs in Delhi, including the closure of 45 metro stations, were being taken to restrict or manage the protesters.His remarks came amid allegations of irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, with more than 13 crore names reportedly deleted from the rolls. Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar has also come under scrutiny following a media report claiming a “rift” between him and the two Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.Responding to the report, the Election Commission said differences of opinion were "normal" in multi-member institutions, adding that all decisions were ultimately taken unanimously.The opposition staged three major protests against the poll body this week. On Saturday, a delegation of the INDIA bloc submitted a memorandum to President Droupadi Murmu, raising its concerns over the issue.(With PTI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: IYC launches legal helpline for protesters detained during CJP protests in Delhi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Indian Youth Congress (IYC) on Saturday launched a legal helpline to assist people facing detention, intimidation or threats linked to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Indian Youth Congress (IYC) on Saturday launched a legal helpline to assist people facing detention, intimidation or threats linked to protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The helpline, 9582223884, will receive complaints from protesters alleging intimidation and harassment over their participation in the demonstrations. It will also facilitate legal assistance for those detained during protests, the Congress' youth wing said.The move comes after Delhi Police detained at least 500 protesters attempting to reach Jantar Mantar for a proposed demonstration called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) against Kumar, sources said.The protesters were detained from several locations across New Delhi, including near Regal Cinema, Minto Bridge and Akashwani Bhawan. Police also deployed drones to monitor the movement of people trying to reach the protest site, they added.Meanwhile, the IYC alleged that police had surrounded its headquarters at 5, Raisina Road, since Friday, with barricades preventing people from entering or leaving the premises.In a post on X, the youth wing accused the authorities of detaining young people, journalists, advocates and Congress workers while failing to act against those allegedly threatening people."Mr Shah, this is Delhi, not your personal police kingdom. Open the gates. Enough of this intimidation," the IYC said, addressing Union Home Minister Amit Shah.Delhi Pradesh Youth Congress president Akshay Lakra also claimed that he had been placed under house arrest.Several IYC workers alleged that they had been detained amid heightened security arrangements in the national capital.The organisation said it would provide support to young people facing action over their participation in the protests and urged those seeking legal assistance to contact the helpline.The protests against the chief election commissioner follow an investigation published by The Indian Express last month. The report claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had objected on record at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders related to the SIR, saying they had been issued without their knowledge or recommendation.The report also said the two commissioners had described specific changes to voter enrolment forms as "unauthorised" and "illegal".The Election Commission has since rejected suggestions of a split within the three-member panel and maintained that decisions relating to the SIR were taken unanimously.(With Agency Inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: 'Nalayak neta': BJP accuses Rahul of dragging President into 'street fights', creating 'anarchy'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday branded Rahul Gandhi a “nalayak neta” over his remarks following the INDIA bloc delegation’s
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday branded Rahul Gandhi a “nalayak neta” over his remarks following the INDIA bloc delegation’s meeting with President Droupadi Murmu. The party accused the Leader of the opposition of misrepresenting the interaction and drawing the country's highest constitutional office into the political row over alleged “vote chori”.Addressing a press briefing, BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra questioned Gandhi’s claim that the President had not denied the Opposition’s allegations of electoral irregularities, arguing that accepting a memorandum did not amount to endorsing its contents.“Yesterday, you saw that some political leaders had gone to Rashtrapati Bhavan. Rahul Gandhi’s statement after coming out of the Rashtrapati Bhavan was equal to that of an incompetent leader 'Nalayak neta,” Patra said.He further accused Gandhi of using inappropriate language against Prime Minister Narendra Modi and constitutional institutions.“He is the Leader of the opposition in the country, but when I say that he is an incompetent leader 'nalayak neta', it is because of the fact that, the entire country watched the kind of abusive language he used against the Prime Minister, the falsehoods he spread against the PM. The country has also witnessed the language you used against India's constitutional offices and institutions,” he said.Patra also accused Rahul Gandhi of attempting to drag President Murmu into what he described as the “anarchy” the Congress leader was seeking to create on the streets of India. Calling Gandhi an “anarchist”, the BJP spokesperson alleged that the Opposition was attempting to turn a constitutional interaction into a political confrontation. “The anarchist Rahul Gandhi tried to pull the President of India into the anarchism which he's trying his best to conduct on the streets of India,” Patra said, adding that there had been no precedent for dragging the President into political street fights.READ ALSO: What’s happening at Jantar Mantar? CJP’s ‘cockroaches’ grounded before anti-SIR showdownQuestioning the Opposition's account of the meeting, Patra said accepting a memorandum was part of the established constitutional protocol and did not amount to endorsing its allegations.“Yet, in the same breath, he claims that the President accepted their memorandum and suggests that she acknowledged their allegations, while also saying that she asked them to provide evidence. Why did they not take the evidence with them? Why did they not present it?” he asked.Patra also challenged the Opposition to present its evidence before the Election Commission of India (ECI), asking, “When the Election Commission of India invites you to appear and present evidence, why do you not go?”Earlier on Friday, Gandhi said on X that the INDIA bloc had submitted a memorandum alleging interference in India's electoral system by Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah and seeking Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.“I was shocked that the President did not deny Vote Chori. Instead, she asked us to bring her proof. We will bring her a mountain of it,” Gandhi wrote.The delegation, led by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and Gandhi, included Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee, Samajwadi Party leader Rajiv Rai, Nationalist Congress Party leader Supriya Sule and National Conference leader Omar Abdullah.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump backs Nidal Hasan’s execution for killing 13 US soldiers, but casts doubt on livestream plan
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has cast doubt on plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former US Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people in a
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has cast doubt on plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former US Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood military base in Texas, even as he backed carrying out the death sentence.Trump said on Friday that authorities were still deciding whether the execution, scheduled for December 3, would be broadcast publicly. The plan has drawn criticism from lawmakers across party lines, human rights groups and religious leaders over concerns about publicly displaying an execution.“They are making a determination about that, but he will be killed,” Trump said. “I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes.”The Pentagon had indicated earlier that the execution would be livestreamed after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the military would ensure people could watch it. However, Vice President JD Vance also expressed uncertainty about whether the broadcast would take place.Vance described Hasan's attack as the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside the September 11, 2001, attacks, but said he would not watch the execution if it was streamed live.The proposed broadcast has faced opposition from both Republicans and Democrats. Republican Representative Austin Scott said Hasan should be executed but argued that livestreaming executions was associated with jihadist groups.Democratic Senator Mark Kelly, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hasan should face justice but questioned whether the United States should associate itself with public executions, comparing the practice to those carried out by Iran and the Taliban.The United Nations human rights office also condemned the proposal. A spokesperson said livestreaming an execution would amount to a public execution and breach the absolute prohibition of torture.Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, called the plan a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death” and said it should be reconsidered.Technology companies YouTube, Meta and X had not immediately responded to requests for comment on whether they would permit the broadcast. TikTok pointed to its policy prohibiting graphic incidents and violence, including the shooting of an individual.Who is Nidal Hasan and what happened at Fort Hood?Hasan, a Virginia native and former Army psychiatrist, fatally shot 13 people and wounded dozens more at Fort Hood on November 5, 2009. Most of those killed were soldiers, and the attack remains one of the deadliest shootings at a US military installation.Hasan was shot by a civilian police officer who responded to the scene and was left paralysed from the waist down.During his 2013 court-martial, Hasan represented himself and did not contest the charges by presenting a defence. He was sentenced to death by a military jury that year. Court-appointed defence lawyers had expressed concerns that he was seeking execution.The court heard that Hasan opposed US military operations in Iraq and Afghanistan and had communicated online with Anwar al-Awlaki, an American-born radical cleric later killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.If carried out as scheduled, Hasan's execution by firing squad would be the first US military firing squad execution since 1945, according to Hegseth. The last US military execution took place in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ukraine war: Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people
articles.summary: Children are among the victims, authorities say, and more victims could still be buried in the rubble of a large apartment block that was destroyed.
articles.body:
Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 15 people including three children, President Volodymyr Zelensky and emergency services have said.

The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the south-eastern city. At least 16 other people were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble after the strike on Saturday morning.

Zelensky said 13 other regions had also been hit overnight, adding: "Our responses to [these] Russian strikes will come".

The Russian attacks happened just hours after President Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US.

Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes show an apartment block mostly destroyed.

"The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed," acting Mayor Regina Kharchenko told Ukrainian television, speaking from the scene.

She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day.

The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble.

Kharchenko said Russia had struck at "our very heart" and "our littlest ones" were among those killed, adding that their deaths were "awful grief for their families. For the city."

Russia targeting 'ordinary life' with attacks on Ukraine's data centres, Zelensky says

Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices

Zelensky has heavily criticised Trump's diesel deal with Russia, calling it a gift to President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".

More recently, in his response to the overnight strikes, he said "Russia interprets any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly continue the war.

"Russia must understand that the war needs to be stopped, and for that, it must feel its losses," he wrote on X .

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months, as the war between the two countries drags on.

Zaporizhzhia is a major regional centre with more than 700,000 residents. It is located less than 10 miles (16 km) from the front line and is frequently attacked by Russian drones and missiles .

The latest strikes on the city comes amid a sharp increase in the number of Russian attacks that are causing higher numbers of civilian casualties.

On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in another Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, in the eastern Donetsk region.

The day before, 22 people including five children died as a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the town of Pryluky, east of Kyiv.

According to the UN, the number of civilian casualties in Ukraine jumped by 55% in the first eight months of this year.

Russia has also targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure , ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.

For its part, Ukraine has attacked Russia's infrastructure - with the latest being strikes on data centres owned by tech giant Yandex .

articles.title: During the pandemic, a US hospital worker paid $15.99 for a Goodwill painting and hung it above her bed; Antiques Roadshow later identified it as a Le Pho worth $60,000-$80,000 at auction
articles.summary: A painting bought for just $15.99 at a Goodwill thrift store turned out to be worth tens of thousands of dollars.
articles.body: A painting bought for just $15.99 at a Goodwill thrift store turned out to be worth tens of thousands of dollars. The buyer, an occupational therapist at a Level I trauma hospital in the United States, had started visiting thrift stores during the COVID-19 pandemic to unwind after demanding days at work. According to PBS’s Antiques Roadshow, she spotted the artwork in the store’s painting section, noticed a plaque on it and decided to take it home. She eventually hung it above her bed, unaware of its potential value. When she brought it for an appraisal in Raleigh, North Carolina, in 2023, an expert identified it as a work by Vietnamese artist Le Pho.A routine thrift-store visit led to an unexpected discoveryThe woman told Antiques Roadshow that shopping at thrift stores had become a way to manage stress while working with patients recovering from serious injuries. On one visit to Goodwill, she noticed a painting that stood out from the other items on display. A small plaque caught her attention because it reminded her of the labels commonly seen beside artworks in museums. She decided to buy the painting for $15.99, without knowing much about its history or the artist behind it.After bringing it home, she hung it above her bed. It remained part of her bedroom decor until she took it to the television programme’s appraisal event at the North Carolina Museum of Art. The painting’s low purchase price made the eventual valuation particularly surprising. What had seemed like an ordinary second-hand find was connected to an artist whose work attracted considerable interest from collectors.The artwork was identified as a Le Pho paintingAt the Raleigh appraisal in 2023, fine-art expert Betty Krulik examined the painting and identified it as Cueillette des Pommes Cannelle, a title translated as “Cinnamon Apple Picking”. The PBS appraisal listing describes the work as an oil painting on board dating to around 1950. During the examination, however, Krulik suggested that it was probably created in the 1960s. The painting carried the artist’s signature in the lower-right corner. A gallery label on the back also provided a useful clue to its history.Krulik connected the work to Findlay Galleries, which had promoted Le Pho’s paintings. Krulik said Findlay Galleries still handled the artist’s estate at the time of the appraisal. The signature, gallery association, medium and size helped explain why the artwork was considered valuable. Le Pho was a Vietnamese-born artist who studied at the École des Beaux-Arts in Hanoi before continuing his artistic education in Paris. He later taught art in Vietnam before settling in Paris, where he developed a style influenced by both Vietnamese traditions and European art. Findlay Galleries helped introduce his paintings to American collectors. Born in 1907, he died in Paris in 2001, and his paintings continue to attract interest in the international art market.An auction estimate of up to $80,000The most startling moment of the appraisal came when Krulik discussed the painting’s potential market value. She estimated that comparable works could sell for between $60,000 and $80,000 at auction. For the owner, that represented an extraordinary difference from the $15.99 she had paid at Goodwill.Krulik also explained that the painting’s size was a positive factor. Although smaller works by Le Pho were available on the market, this painting was a standard size for the artist and belonged to a period that collectors particularly valued. The expert offered a separate figure for insurance purposes, suggesting coverage closer to $100,000 if the owner wanted to insure the work. These figures were estimates rather than a confirmed sale price. The painting was not reported as having sold for $60,000 to $80,000; the appraisal indicated what it might fetch at auction based on comparable works.Why the thrift-store find mattersThe discovery highlights how the value of an artwork can be difficult to judge from its appearance or the price attached to it in a second-hand shop. A signature, a gallery label and an expert’s knowledge of an artist’s career can reveal information that an ordinary buyer might overlook. In this case, the owner had purchased the painting for personal enjoyment and displayed it above her bed without knowing its potential significance. The appraisal gave her a very different understanding of the artwork she had lived with.The story also demonstrates the importance of provenance and specialist assessment in the art market. Even when an artist is established, a painting’s value depends on factors such as its authenticity, condition, dimensions and place within the artist’s career. For the hospital worker, a $15.99 purchase made during a stressful period became an unexpected discovery. What began as a way to unwind after work led to an artwork that an expert valued at tens of thousands of dollars.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Last I heard, India was democratic': Former cricketer Sanjay Manjrekar reacts to CJP protest crackdown in Delhi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former Indian cricketer Sanjay Manjrekar on Saturday weighed in on the police action against protesters from the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Indian cricketer Sanjay Manjrekar on Saturday weighed in on the police action against protesters from the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Delhi, saying peaceful protests were a democratic activity.“Peaceful protests is a democratic activity. Last time I heard India was a democratic country,” Manjrekar posted on X, amid heightened security in the capital ahead of the CJP’s proposed ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ demonstration demanding chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.The protest, planned for Saturday, was called to raise allegations of irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Delhi Police had denied permission for the demonstration, citing public safety, traffic management and law-and-order concerns.Stone pelting reported near Akashwani BhawanStone pelting was reported near Akashwani Bhawan during the protest, leaving two police personnel injured. Several protesters were detained as security personnel moved to control the situation.Sub-inspector Bajrang Jadhav was among those injured. Asked how he sustained his injuries, he said, “I was pushed me, while apprehending the rioters, this caused an injury.”Police had deployed personnel across the capital, erected barricades and intensified checks at entry points ahead of the planned demonstration.CJP leaders detained ahead of ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, co-convenor Saurav Das and leader Ashutosh Ranka were detained after arriving in Delhi. A video from a Delhi-bound flight showed Dipke challenging police personnel to arrest him and questioning the grounds for his detention.“Come on, arrest us! We have come here to get arrested. We are not afraid of you. Arrest us!” he said.In the video, Dipke also described the police action as “dictatorship” and repeatedly asked to speak to senior male officers as women police personnel surrounded him.YouTuber Dhruv Rathee was also detained from his residence in Gurgaon ahead of the proposed protest.Over 1,500 detained across DelhiMore than 1,500 people had been detained from different parts of Delhi ahead of the planned demonstration as police stepped up preventive measures.The CJP has been demanding Kumar’s removal over alleged voter-list manipulation and has called for accountability over the SIR exercise.
